item.title: Alibaba’s Chip Unit Wants to Go Public. Who Pays It?
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication. item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article is republished from Jumpstart, a TechNode Group publication.

Alibaba says more than 60% of T-Head’s computing capacity serves customers outside the group. Some of them are carmakers that use its Zhenwu chips to develop driver-assistance systems. They can do that by renting computing power from Alibaba Cloud, without ever buying a chip from T-Head. For Alibaba, that is a sale. For someone buying shares in T-Head, the question is how much of that sale belongs to the chip company. Alibaba disclosed both figures in its fiscal-year update.

On November 10, Alibaba confirmed that T-Head had filed confidentially for a Hong Kong listing in September. Alibaba would retain control. International Financing Review reported that the IPO could raise at least US$2 billion. Estimates of what the whole company is worth vary widely. JPMorgan reportedly estimated its value at US$25 billion to US$62 billion, while Nomura reportedly put it at US$85 billion. Before investors can settle on a price, they need a clearer picture of how much business T-Head does on its own.

Why Alibaba wants to list it

T-Head began in 2018 as Alibaba’s chip design arm. It now makes Zhenwu processors for training and running AI models and Yitian CPUs for cloud servers. It also licenses Xuantie processor designs, based on the open RISC-V standard, to companies building their own chips. Earlier this year, Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu put T-Head’s annualised revenue at around RMB10 billion.

Alibaba is still bringing the two businesses closer together. In August, it said it had combined Alibaba Cloud and T-Head into one reporting segment. A month later, it unveiled a server that brings together T-Head’s next AI processor, networking hardware and storage controller. The cloud business gives the chip team somewhere to deploy new designs at scale, and the chip team gives Alibaba more control over what goes into its data centres.

That arrangement takes money. Alibaba reported a free cash outflow of nearly RMB45 billion in the June quarter and attributed the deterioration mainly to higher spending on cloud infrastructure. A listing would let T-Head raise money from investors of its own while Alibaba keeps control and continues to use its chips.

Whose customers are they?

Alibaba Cloud has already done something valuable for T-Head. It has put the chips in front of companies with real work to run. By August, Alibaba said more than 650 external customers had adopted the Zhenwu M890 through its cloud services. A carmaker can start a training job on a chip it has never used before without buying servers or setting up a new data centre.

Now follow the payment. When that carmaker rents computing power from Alibaba Cloud, the cloud business bills it. How much does Alibaba Cloud pay T-Head for the chips? How much of T-Head’s revenue comes from those sales within the group? And how much comes from customers that buy chips, systems or processor designs directly from T-Head? Alibaba’s listing announcement leaves those questions open.

Selling through Alibaba Cloud can be a good business for T-Head. The cloud brings in customers and gives the chip team a reason to keep improving its products. But an investor needs to know how that arrangement works for the company whose shares they will own. A chip order from a customer outside Alibaba and a chip order from Alibaba Cloud can both end up serving the same kind of AI workload. They tell investors different things about who sets the price and who decides whether to place the next order.

What to look for in the prospectus

The first thing to look for is a breakdown of who pays T-Head. How much comes directly from customers outside Alibaba, what do they buy, and do they come back for more? The terms of its business with Alibaba Cloud matter too. Together, those disclosures would give investors a clearer picture of where T-Head earns its money today and what could grow from here.

The second is what customers build with Xuantie. T-Head lists uses ranging from storage to industrial networking. The next signal would be a carmaker, robotics company or cloud provider choosing a Xuantie design for a product it expects to sell and support for years. A chip running inside Alibaba’s cloud shows what T-Head can build with its parent. A customer building its own product around a T-Head design shows what it is willing to build with T-Head.

item.title: DJI to revise prices on some products as chip and memory costs climb
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: DJI said Friday it will change suggested retail prices for some products starting November 18, citing sustained increases in the cost of semiconductors, memory and other key components. The changes take effect at midnight, according to a notice posted on DJI’s Chinese website. The notice did not list the affected models or specify how much […]
item.content:encoded:
DJI said Friday it will change suggested retail prices for some products starting November 18, citing sustained increases in the cost of semiconductors, memory and other key components. The changes take effect at midnight, according to a notice posted on DJI’s Chinese website.

The notice did not list the affected models or specify how much prices would change. DJI directed customers to individual product pages in its official store for updated prices. [IT Home, in Chinese]

item.title: BYD’s Denza launches five-seat N8 SUV with up to 1,003 km of electric range
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: BYD’s premium brand Denza has launched the N8 in China, with prices ranging from RMB 269,900 to RMB 329,900. The five-seat SUV comes in four battery-electric and two plug-in hybrid versions. Its longest-range electric variant pairs rear-wheel drive with a 130.15 kWh Blade Battery and is rated for 1,003 km under China’s CLTC test cycle. […]
item.content:encoded:
BYD’s premium brand Denza has launched the N8 in China, with prices ranging from RMB 269,900 to RMB 329,900. The five-seat SUV comes in four battery-electric and two plug-in hybrid versions. Its longest-range electric variant pairs rear-wheel drive with a 130.15 kWh Blade Battery and is rated for 1,003 km under China’s CLTC test cycle.

At 5.15 meters long, the N8 is 50 mm shorter than the N8L while retaining the same 3.075-meter wheelbase. Inside, a 1.1-meter head-up display projects speed and navigation information into the driver’s field of view, and a 30-inch dashboard screen supports split-screen use. All versions come with BYD’s God’s Eye 5.0 driver-assistance system, which supports assisted driving on highways and city streets, as well as automated parking. [Sina Auto, in Chinese]

item.title: MetaX and UBTech-backed robotics chip startup Xilect raises RMB 500 million
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Xilect, a robotics chip startup jointly founded by Chinese GPU maker MetaX and humanoid robot maker UBTech Robotics, has raised RMB 500 million in an angel round. The company will use the funding to develop its first chip and supporting software, expand its engineering team and test the platform with robot manufacturers. Xilect is designing […]
item.content:encoded:
Xilect, a robotics chip startup jointly founded by Chinese GPU maker MetaX and humanoid robot maker UBTech Robotics, has raised RMB 500 million in an angel round. The company will use the funding to develop its first chip and supporting software, expand its engineering team and test the platform with robot manufacturers.

Xilect is designing a system-on-chip that combines multimodal perception, decision-making and motion control on the robot itself. Its software toolchain is intended to help robot makers run existing AI models on the platform. The startup plans to give partners a development and testing platform in 2027 and release its first chip in 2028. [Xilect, in Chinese]

item.title: Xiaohongshu tests standalone app for users to build and share AI agents
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Xiaohongshu, the Chinese social platform also known as RedNote, is testing a standalone app called Dada that lets users turn their expertise into AI agents others can use. Ebrun found dozens of agents in the app, covering tasks such as design, job hunting and studying. Users can interact with them through text and images. Dada […]
item.content:encoded:
Xiaohongshu, the Chinese social platform also known as RedNote, is testing a standalone app called Dada that lets users turn their expertise into AI agents others can use. Ebrun found dozens of agents in the app, covering tasks such as design, job hunting and studying. Users can interact with them through text and images.

Dada also lets users bring agents into group chats with friends and share invitations through WeChat. The format gives creators a way to turn the kind of advice they already share in Xiaohongshu posts into tools that can answer follow-up questions and work with material users upload. [Ebrun, in Chinese]

item.title: ByteDance’s AI chip chief has submitted his resignation, report says
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Shi Yunfeng, who leads ByteDance’s AI chip and data processing unit teams, has submitted his resignation and is handing over his responsibilities, LatePost reported. Shi joined ByteDance in 2018 and reports to Yang Zhenyuan, who heads the company’s cloud business, Volcano Engine. ByteDance began building its AI chip team in 2019 and pursued a custom […]
item.content:encoded:
Shi Yunfeng, who leads ByteDance’s AI chip and data processing unit teams, has submitted his resignation and is handing over his responsibilities, LatePost reported. Shi joined ByteDance in 2018 and reports to Yang Zhenyuan, who heads the company’s cloud business, Volcano Engine.

ByteDance began building its AI chip team in 2019 and pursued a custom accelerator modeled on Google’s Tensor Processing Units. The aim was to improve performance and power efficiency for its own AI workloads. The chip reached tape-out this year, but its performance fell short of expectations, according to the report. The team is now developing a successor. [LatePost, in Chinese]

item.title: When robots dive underwater, HeymanDex sees new possibilities for dexterous hands
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: Dexterous hands are becoming a new focus of competition in the humanoid robotics industry. Companies are working to improve robots’ hand capabilities in terms of degrees of freedom, gripping force and movement precision. But as robots move beyond controlled laboratory environments, a new question emerges: can their hands still function properly when performing everyday tasks […]
item.content:encoded:
Dexterous hands are becoming a new focus of competition in the humanoid robotics industry. Companies are working to improve robots’ hand capabilities in terms of degrees of freedom, gripping force and movement precision.

But as robots move beyond controlled laboratory environments, a new question emerges: can their hands still function properly when performing everyday tasks such as washing dishes and vegetables, or even carrying out delicate operations underwater?

To explore this question, we had the opportunity to interview the team at HeymanDex, learning how the robotics company is entering the dexterous hand market through underwater applications, as well as the technology strategy and commercialization plans behind its approach.

Unlike most dexterous hand manufacturers that focus on land-based applications, HeymanDex has taken a different approach by prioritizing protection capabilities to improve the reliability of robotic hands in challenging environments.

From deep-sea equipment to robotic hands: why go underwater?

Competition in the dexterous hand industry has largely focused on performance indicators such as degrees of freedom, fingertip force and response speed. HeymanDex, however, has chosen a differentiated path, making underwater environments a key starting point for its product development.

The choice reflects the team’s background in underwater and specialized robotics. HeymanDex’s core team has previously worked on projects involving 8,000-meter-class deep-sea landers and sampling equipment for the Jiaolong manned submersible. This experience has given the team a practical understanding of the engineering challenges involved in underwater operations, particularly water pressure, corrosion and sealing.

In the team’s view, robots must be able to operate beyond dry, flat laboratory settings if they are to become truly general-purpose machines. Everyday household tasks such as washing vegetables and dishes, industrial processes involving cutting fluids and lubricants, and deep-sea engineering operations all place demands on a robot’s ability to withstand harsh environments.

HeymanDex therefore aims to make protection capabilities a fundamental part of dexterous hands rather than an additional feature.

The core technical challenge lies in keeping dexterous hands flexible underwater

For a multi-jointed dexterous hand, waterproofing is far more complicated than simply adding a sealed outer casing. The fingers need to bend and extend continuously, while multiple internal joints and transmission mechanisms must remain flexible. Achieving reliable dynamic sealing in these moving components without compromising transmission efficiency is one of the biggest engineering challenges.

HeymanDex identifies its independently developed underwater integrated dynamic sealing technology system as a key technical advantage. The company has developed two technical solutions for different water-depth requirements.

For depths of 0 to 1,000 meters, its technology covers high-linear-speed axial dynamic sealing, high-reliability radial static sealing and magnetic-coupling dynamic sealing. For ultra-deep-sea environments ranging from 1,000 to 10,000 meters, the company has further developed technologies including hydraulic dynamic pressure compensation, oil-filled magnetic-coupling dynamic pressure balancing and dual-stage static sealing.

The company also optimizes materials, manufacturing processes and overall product design to improve corrosion resistance and long-term operating reliability.

In simple terms, conventional dexterous hands mainly focus on gripping objects more accurately and moving faster. Underwater dexterous hands must achieve the same capabilities while ensuring stable operation under sustained water pressure and other challenging environmental conditions.

WA100 moves from prototype testing to real-world applications

HeymanDex has launched its first commercial product, the WA100 underwater dexterous hand. According to company-provided data, the standard engineering configuration supports operations at depths of up to 300 meters. Customized versions can also be developed for different depth requirements, ranging from 100 meters to 10,000 meters.

The WA100 features a five-finger structure with six active degrees of freedom and 11 linked joints. It weighs no more than 1,250 grams, delivers a minimum output force of 10N per finger and supports a total pulling load of at least 5 kilograms.

According to HeymanDex, the WA100 has completed 500,000 durability test movements without damage. The company also says its dynamic sealing system has an effective service life of up to 4,000 hours, while the complete system can operate continuously for hundreds of hours without failure. HeymanDex further claims that the product achieves an 80% success rate in underwater operations and offers around five times the generalization capability of conventional two-finger grippers.

The WA100 primarily targets universities and research institutes, customers requiring specialized operations, and manufacturers of underwater robots, robotic arms and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs). HeymanDex is also working with a leading domestic pool-cleaning robot manufacturer to explore applications in underwater cleaning and equipment maintenance.

The commercialization of its first product marks the company’s transition from technical development and prototype validation toward product delivery. However, improving reliability, controlling costs and expanding its customer base remain important challenges.

Expanding from underwater robotics to wider applications

HeymanDex does not intend to limit its business to underwater applications. Instead, it hopes to use underwater technology as a starting point and extend its underlying capabilities in sealing, drive systems, transmission and control to a wider range of robotic products.

The company has begun expanding into industrial manufacturing, general-purpose commercial applications, and research and education. Its Dasheng 1 industrial dexterous hand, for example, is exploring the integration of multiple configurations with industrial manipulation requirements.

Overseas markets are also part of the company’s expansion strategy. The WA100 was previously showcased at IFA in Berlin, Germany, while the Dasheng 1 industrial dexterous hand appeared at IROS in the US. The company has also begun product adaptation work with a leading German robotics company and is focusing on markets in the US, Europe and Japan.

By entering the technically demanding underwater market, HeymanDex is seeking to build a technology platform that can eventually be applied across a wider range of industries.

In the future, robots may work not only on factory production lines but also in homes, hospitals, oceans and even more extreme environments. As robots take on increasingly complex real-world tasks, simply being able to grasp an object will no longer be enough. The real challenge for the next generation of dexterous hands may be ensuring that they can perform tasks reliably and consistently across different environments.

item.title: In Nvidia’s Shadow, a Chinese Chipmaker Takes a Different Route
item.dc:creator: Lucia
item.description: Editor’s note: Denglin Technology, a Chinese maker of general-purpose GPUs for AI computing, went public in Hong Kong on November 10, raising HK$1.41 billion. Revenue reached RMB 200.4 million in the first four months of 2026, already exceeding its full-year 2025 total. Frost & Sullivan ranked it third in China’s enterprise AI GPGPU market, but […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: Denglin Technology, a Chinese maker of general-purpose GPUs for AI computing, went public in Hong Kong on November 10, raising HK$1.41 billion. Revenue reached RMB 200.4 million in the first four months of 2026, already exceeding its full-year 2025 total. Frost & Sullivan ranked it third in China’s enterprise AI GPGPU market, but its share was just 1%. Can the newly listed chipmaker turn rapid growth into lasting market clout?

From meeting-note assistants to factory cameras and exam-monitoring systems, AI increasingly runs on GPUs. For chipmakers, building a processor is only half the job; the harder part is winning customers from established suppliers such as Nvidia.

A Different Kind of Memory Bet

Founded in Shanghai in 2017 by four former colleagues at embedded-GPU developer Vivante, Denglin spent six months visiting customers and suppliers before settling on a design combining general-purpose computing with AI acceleration.

The team initially targeted smart-city applications, with its first chip samples arriving in early 2021. As the business expanded, it moved its headquarters to Suzhou in 2024, closer to the semiconductor supply chain.

An early choice reflected Denglin’s strategy: smartphone-style low-power double data rate (LPDDR) over the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) common in high-end accelerators. LPDDR is cheaper, more energy-efficient and offers greater supply-chain control, but its lower bandwidth can bottleneck the largest AI models.

Denglin sought to ease this bottleneck with more on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) and software that reuses data rather than repeatedly fetching it from external memory. The design prioritizes cost and power efficiency over peak performance.

In October, Denglin’s KS GPUs had completed compatibility testing and efficiency optimization for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, demonstrating their ability to support a major AI model.

Denglin also plans to move into higher-performance AI computing. The first Minsky IV version is planned for December 2026, while a second version, targeted for the second half of 2027, is expected to adopt HBM3e or other advanced memory for large AI data centers and public clouds.

Betting on a Smaller Cloud

For now, Denglin’s efficiency-focused GPUs are best suited to enterprise AI, particularly private clouds, where customers value cost, power efficiency and data control. Its products also target edge inference and terminal devices.

Enterprise AI was still a relatively small segment, accounting for 9.5% of China’s general purpose graphics processing units (GPGPU) market in 2025, compared with 90.5% for public-cloud AI, according to Frost & Sullivan estimates.

Denglin’s own business has since shifted in that direction. In 2023, smart-city projects generated about 80% of its GPGPU product revenue.

But by the first four months of 2026, enterprise private cloud accounted for 83%, while smart cities contributed just 12.2%. Its KS inference cards helped drive the shift: Denglin sold 10,246 during the period, generating RMB166 million.

The shift coincided with rapid revenue growth. Sales climbed from RMB27.9 million in 2023 to RMB82.6 million in 2024 and RMB171.3 million in 2025, before reaching RMB200.4 million in just the first four months of 2026.

The competitive gap remains wide, however. Frost & Sullivan ranked Denglin third in China’s enterprise AI GPGPU market by 2025 revenue. Yet it held just 1% market share, compared with Nvidia’s 83.1% and AMD’s 12.3%.

Growth With a Catch

Rapid sales growth has yet to translate into sustained profitability. Denglin recorded net losses RMB332 million in 2023, RMB 296.5 million in 2024 and RMB281 million in 2025. Heavy R&D spending was a major factor: in 2025, it reached RMB238 million, nearly three times the company’s gross profit of RMB84.3 million.

The picture improved in the first four months of 2026, when its net loss fell to RMB16.5 million from RMB108.3 million a year earlier. Adjusted net profit reached RMB20.6 million after adding back share-based payment and listing expenses.

But another challenge lies in its customer base. Its five largest customers accounted for 90.4% of revenue in the first four months of 2026, with the biggest contributing 38%. Converting early adoption into repeat orders and broadening its customer base will be crucial to sustaining growth.

The Public-Market Test

On November 10, Denglin listed in Hong Kong, raising about HK$1.415 billion. It went public under Chapter 18C, which allows specialist-technology companies that have yet to meet the exchange’s HK$250 million annual revenue threshold to list as pre-commercial issuers.

The company plans to use 35% of net proceeds to upgrade existing GPU lines, 25% to develop new product categories and 20% on software tools.

AI is already moving into factories and offices. Denglin has gained a foothold, but turning early adoption into repeat business and lasting competitiveness is a different challenge.

item.title: Baidu’s Robin Li says AI’s next phase is the “intelligent organization,” outlines three principles
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Baidu founder Robin Li said Thursday that the next stage of AI adoption will require companies to redesign how they work. Speaking at Baidu World 2026 in Beijing, he laid out three principles for what he calls an “intelligent organization”: organize work around tasks that cross job boundaries, document employee know-how so teams and AI […]
item.content:encoded:
Baidu founder Robin Li said Thursday that the next stage of AI adoption will require companies to redesign how they work. Speaking at Baidu World 2026 in Beijing, he laid out three principles for what he calls an “intelligent organization”: organize work around tasks that cross job boundaries, document employee know-how so teams and AI agents can reuse it, and measure the results of each workflow so it can be improved over time.

Li said jobs would increasingly fall into two broad groups. He described “builders” as people who create products or services and “sellers” as people whose work depends on communication and trust. The distinction was part of his argument that companies could assign work by task as AI takes on more steps across teams.

Li pointed to Baidu’s own operations as an early example. Over the past year, the number of AI agents active daily inside the company rose from about 5,000 to 37,000, while the number of tasks they completed each week increased from 84,000 to more than 1 million, according to Baidu. [TechNode reporting]

item.title: ByteDance reportedly plans AI assistant similar to Meta’s Muse
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: ByteDance plans to introduce an AI assistant similar to Meta’s Muse in the coming weeks, IT Home reported on Wednesday, citing Bloomberg. ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming outlined the plan at an internal meeting with the company’s AI team, according to people familiar with the discussion. Meta launched Muse in September as a voice-based assistant with […]
item.content:encoded:
ByteDance plans to introduce an AI assistant similar to Meta’s Muse in the coming weeks, IT Home reported on Wednesday, citing Bloomberg. ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming outlined the plan at an internal meeting with the company’s AI team, according to people familiar with the discussion.

Meta launched Muse in September as a voice-based assistant with an animated avatar and plans to bring it to devices including smart glasses. ByteDance already operates the Doubao chatbot and sells access to its Seedance video generation models. The new assistant would expand its consumer AI lineup.

At the meeting, Zhang said ByteDance could compete with OpenAI and Anthropic but estimated it would take until 2029 or 2030 to reach their level. He pointed to a gap in pretraining data and urged the team to rely less on distillation, a technique that trains one model on another model’s outputs. [IT Home, in Chinese]
